# Light and Telescopes

Almost everything we know about the universe arrived as light. Before you read
on, predict: if you move a lamp twice as far away, does it look half as
bright, a quarter as bright, or the same? Make the bet.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- order the electromagnetic spectrum by wavelength, frequency and energy;
- use the inverse-square law to compare brightness at different distances;
- explain why a telescope's aperture matters more than its magnification.

## The Spectrum {#the-electromagnetic-spectrum}

Light is an electromagnetic wave traveling at about 300,000 km/s. Its
**wavelength** is the distance from one crest to the next; its **frequency** is
how many crests pass each second. Wavelength times frequency equals the speed
of light, so a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency.

Light also arrives in packets of energy called **photons**, and a shorter
wavelength photon carries more energy. That is why ultraviolet light can burn
your skin and radio waves cannot.

From longest to shortest wavelength, the spectrum runs:

> radio, microwave, infrared, **visible**, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray

Visible light runs from red (about 700 nm) to violet (about 400 nm). Picture a
piano keyboard miles long: our eyes hear about one octave of it.

Every warm object glows, and the hotter it is, the shorter the wavelength of
its peak glow. A stove burner goes dull red, then orange, then yellow-white as
it heats. In astronomy, red means cool and blue means hot. You glow too, in
the infrared, which is how thermal cameras see people in the dark.

Our atmosphere lets visible light and most radio waves through, absorbs much
of the infrared, and blocks ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. To see in
those bands, telescopes have to go to space.

## Brightness Falls Off With Distance {#the-inverse-square-law}

Light leaving a lamp spreads out over a sphere. The area of that sphere grows
as the distance squared, so the light landing on each square meter falls off
as **one over the distance squared**:

| Distance | Apparent brightness |
|---|---|
| 1 times | 1 |
| 2 times | 1/4 |
| 3 times | 1/9 |
| 10 times | 1/100 |

So the answer to the opening bet is a quarter, not a half. A flashlight beam
at twice the distance covers four times the area, and each patch gets a
quarter of the light.

The rule works backwards too, which is the whole point for astronomers. Two
identical streetlights stand along a straight road, and the far one looks one
sixteenth as bright. It must be four times farther away, because 4 squared is
16. Know how bright a light really is, measure how bright it looks, and you
know how far away it is.

## Bigger Is Better {#telescopes}

A telescope has three jobs. In order of importance:

1. **Gather light.** Its light-gathering power depends on the area of its main
   lens or mirror, the **aperture**, so it grows with the diameter squared. A
   telescope twice as wide collects four times as much light. A 2-meter mirror
   collects about 80,000 times as much as your 7-millimeter pupil.
2. **Resolve detail.** A bigger aperture also separates finer details.
3. **Magnify.** This only enlarges whatever the first two jobs delivered.

A telescope is a bucket for light: a bucket twice as wide catches four times
the rain. Magnification is the number printed biggest on department-store
telescope boxes, and it matters least. Stars stay points of light at any
magnification, and too much magnification just spreads a faint, blurry image
over a bigger area.

::: {.callout-warning title="Eye safety"}
Never point a telescope or binoculars at the Sun unless a proper solar filter
covers the front. A telescope gathers light; aimed at the Sun, it gathers
enough to blind you instantly.
:::

## Self-check

```{=html}
<div class="quiz" data-answer="c">
  <div class="question">1. A star is moved to three times its current distance. Its apparent brightness becomes:</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> One third as bright</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> One sixth as bright</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> One ninth as bright</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> Unchanged, only smaller</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>c</strong>. Brightness goes as one over distance squared: 3 squared is 9.
  </div>
</div>

<div class="quiz" data-answer="b">
  <div class="question">2. Telescope A has a 10 cm aperture at 300x. Telescope B has a 30 cm aperture at 100x. Which shows fainter galaxies?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> A, because it magnifies more</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> B, because it gathers 9 times the light</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> B, because it gathers 3 times the light</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> They are equal</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>b</strong>. Light-gathering power goes as the aperture squared: (30/10) squared is 9. You can always change the eyepiece; you cannot change the aperture.
  </div>
</div>
```

## Where this fits

AST 102 leans on all three ideas: a star's color gives its temperature, the
inverse-square law links brightness and distance, and big telescopes are how
we gather the light of distant galaxies.
